newsitem.title: UK: Labour government pledges high-skill economy.
newsitem.headline: Labour government pledges high-skill economy.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government pledged on Sunday to build a "high-skill, high-investment" economy and establish new partnerships with business.

In an open letter to thousands of firms throughout the country, Trade and Industry Secretary Margaret Beckett said she wanted her department "to build a real partnership with every part of industry, so our businesses can prosper and thrive".
"This means building a high investment, high skill, sustainable economy through open and competitive markets at home and abroad," she said.

"Before we came to power, we consulted extensively with all sectors of the business community. Now that we are in government we shall build on that consultation, working closely with Britain's entrepreneurs."

Under reformist leader Tony Blair, Labour worked hard to win the trust of British business and the City of London financial district and convince them that it was committed to prudent economic policies. It succeeded to a remarkable extent, winning open support from some top executives.
London's stock and bond markets rallied on Friday after Blair's landslide election win on Thursday, reflecting the fact that markets have also largely lost their fear of Labour.
Beckett's letter promised particular help for Britain's exporters, who are struggling with a strong pound which has made their goods much more expensive abroad.
"We are particularly keen to work in partnership with Britain's exporters and to expand the number of companies, small and large, who are exporting," she said.

The Labour government's policies on the European Union would also be tailored to British business needs, including a drive to complete the bloc's Single Market, giving British manufacturers open access to all corners of the EU market.
"We need to give Britain new leadership and to drive for the early completion of the Single Market," Beckett said.

Turning to two key Labour policies which business leaders are suspicious of, Beckett confirmed Labour's commitment to a minimum wage and signing up to the European Union Social Chapter, which guarantees minimum employment rights.
She said these would be positive for industry, helping to foster good employer-employee relations.

"In our high-skill economy, I want us to have the benefits of stable and co-operative relations between employees and employers. The Social Chapter and the national minimum wage are tools we should use to help us achieve this," she said.

On Friday, employer groups such as the Confederation of British Industry and British Chambers of Commerce congratulated the Labour Party on its crushing election victory but voiced concerns about the level of the minimum wage, the Social Chapter and Labour's planned windfall tax on privatised utilities.
Beckett's letter also promised a "simple, helpful and fair" regulation structure and pledged to introduce a regional support scheme to give small firms a helping hand.
"At home, where small and growing firms are the bedrock of a successful enterprise economy, we shall improve the quality of our support in the regions," she said.
"We have already started discussions with organisations representing small business and with some local authorities about cutting red tape and encouraging enterprise."

All this would create a dynamic environment in which go-getting entrepreneurs could look to the future with confidence, she said. "Britain is a great place to do business and the best base from which to compete internationally."
